memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: Abram and Nahor both married. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife was Milkah... Now Sarai was childless because she was not able to conceive. - Gen 11:29-30 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
And now the sentence that shapes everything that follows: "Sarai was childless because she was not able to conceive." Just as God is about to promise Abram countless descendants, we learn that his wife cannot have children. The human situation is impossible. The promise of a great nation rests on a barren womb.

This is not accidental. Scripture places this fact here deliberately, so that when God's promise comes, we know beyond doubt that its fulfilment will be God's work, not human achievement. Where Babel said "let us make a name for ourselves," God will build a nation out of a couple who cannot even have one child.

If you are living with a longing unfulfilled - for a child, a healing, a restored relationship, a door that will not open - this verse speaks to you. Sarai's barrenness was real, painful, and long. God did not deny her sorrow or hurry it away. She would wait many years still.

But her emptiness became the very stage for God's power. God delights to work where human ability has run out, "so that no one may boast before him" (1 Cor 1:29). Paul writes that God "gives life to the dead and calls into being things that were not" (Rom 4:17) - speaking precisely of Abraham and Sarah. Your barren places are not beyond God. They may be exactly where He intends to display His grace.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Where are you waiting in a season that feels barren or impossible?
- Can you trust God to work where human ability has run out?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, You work where human strength has failed and call into being things that were not. Meet me in my barren places, and let Your power be displayed where I have nothing left to give.
Amen.
